opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think you have to understand the incentive structure, because it's not quite what people assume. A lot of venture capitalists aren't actually betting that the technology will work in the way it's being advertised. They're betting that they can get out before anybody notices whether it does.

If you're a VC, you get paid on management fees, typically a couple of percent of the fund every year, regardless of outcome. So the bigger the fund, the more money you make, and the way you raise a bigger fund is by being in the hot sector. Right now the hot sector is generative AI, so there's enormous pressure to have exposure to it. Nobody gets fired for investing in the thing everybody else is investing in. If it blows up, well, everybody got it wrong together. If you sat it out and it worked, you look like an idiot. That asymmetry drives a lot of herd behavior.

Then there's the valuation game. You don't need the company to be profitable; you need the next round to come in at a higher price. As long as there's a story — scaling is going to get us to AGI, the next model will fix the hallucinations — the markups keep coming, and on paper everybody looks brilliant. The question is what happens when the story stops being credible, and I've been saying for a long time that the story has real problems. These systems still hallucinate, still struggle with reliable reasoning, still don't have robust world models. And the economics are rough: the training costs are huge, inference isn't free, the models are increasingly commoditized, and there's price competition that drives margins toward zero. When five or six companies have roughly the same thing, nobody has a moat.

There's also a degree of genuine belief, and I don't want to be uncharitable. Some of these people really do think that if you just add more data and more compute, intelligence falls out. I think that's an empirical hypothesis that's been looking worse and worse, with diminishing returns showing up in exactly the way some of us predicted. But if you've built your identity and your portfolio around it, it's very hard to update.

So my short answer is: a mix of misaligned incentives, herd behavior, fear of missing out, and a sincere but, I think, mistaken faith in scaling. None of that requires the underlying business to make sense. It just requires the music to keep playing a little longer. And historically, that's how bubbles work. The technology isn't worthless — there are real uses — but the valuations are priced as if we're about to get general intelligence, and I don't think we're anywhere close to that with the current approach.

r001.rationale: The response says VCs earn management fees based on fund size regardless of outcome, and describes investment stories that sustain markups even when profitability is not required.

r002.rationale: It says generative AI is the hot sector and describes AGI and scaling narratives that make investments seem promising and support higher valuations.

r003.rationale: The response discusses venture capitalists generally seeking to exit before a bubble is noticed, but does not mention pension-fund participation or its managers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I'd say that venture capital has never been primarily in the business of being right. It's in the business of being right occasionally, in a very big way, and being wrong a lot of the time in ways that are survivable. So if you're a VC and you think there's a five or ten percent chance that one of these companies becomes the next Google, you put money in, and the fact that I think the other ninety percent is going to zero doesn't really trouble you. That's the model. It's a power-law bet, not a careful appraisal of whether the technology does what it's claimed to do.

The second thing is that there's an enormous amount of FOMO. Nobody wants to be the firm that passed on the thing everybody's talking about. I've talked to people in that world, and a lot of them will privately say, "Look, I'm not sure the unit economics work, I'm not sure the hallucination problem gets solved, but I can't not be in it." That's a herd dynamic, not an analysis. We saw the same thing with crypto, we saw it with the dot-com bubble, we saw it with driverless cars, where I was saying in 2016 that the last one percent was going to be really hard, and billions went in on the assumption it would be done by 2020.

And the third thing, honestly, is that the money is being made right now in ways that don't require the technology to work. If you can raise at a higher valuation than you came in at, you've done your job, in a sense. There's a greater-fool element to it. The question of whether large language models are actually reliable enough to automate the things people are promising, whether the cost of inference ever gets covered by what people will pay, whether you've got a moat when everyone's training on roughly the same data, those are questions that get pushed down the road as long as the next round closes.

So I don't think the funding tells us much about the science. It tells us about incentives. The capital flowing in is not evidence that the problems I've been pointing to, the lack of robust reasoning, the lack of a world model, the brittleness, have been solved. It's evidence that a lot of people are hoping they'll be solved before the music stops. And some of them will be fine either way, because they'll have gotten out. It's the people holding the bag at the end, and I'd argue the broader public who's been told that AGI is around the corner, who I actually worry about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses power-law bets and valuation gains, but does not mention management fees or explain that fees reward arranging large investments regardless of profitability.

r002.rationale: It describes FOMO and herd dynamics around AI, but does not clearly say AI hype makes large investments sound plausible to venture capitalists.

r003.rationale: It says some investors may be fine because they will have gotten out, but does not identify pension funds or their managers as expecting to exit before a collapse.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between whether a technology is going to transform the economy and whether a venture capitalist can make money investing in it. Those are different questions. You can make money if you get in early and sell your stake at a higher valuation, even if the underlying business never becomes sustainable.

And venture capital is a portfolio game. You can lose on a lot of bets if one turns out to be enormously successful. So if you think there’s even a small chance that one of these companies will dominate a huge market, you may invest despite serious doubts about the economics today.

Then there’s fear of missing out. Nobody wants to be the person who passed on the next Google. That doesn’t mean every investor is irrational. It means their incentives don’t necessarily line up with the question I’m asking: Can these systems deliver reliable value at a price customers will pay, with enough margin to cover their costs? A large funding round doesn’t answer that question.

r001.rationale: The response mentions selling a stake at a higher valuation, but does not say management fees reward arranging large investments regardless of profitability.

r002.rationale: It cites the chance of a company dominating a market and fear of missing out, but does not identify AI hype as making large investments sound plausible.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention pension funds or managers expecting to leave before investments collapse.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the incentives for a venture capitalist are different from the incentives for somebody asking whether this is a sustainable business. You can make money on an investment if you get in early and sell at a higher valuation, even if the underlying economics never really work out.

And there’s a portfolio argument: most of your bets can fail if one pays off enormously. If you think there’s even a small chance that one of these companies will dominate a huge market, you may be willing to take that risk.

But we should distinguish willingness to fund something from evidence that it works economically. The questions are still: How much does it cost to deliver the service? What will customers actually pay? And what happens to your margins if competitors offer essentially the same thing? Excitement about the technology doesn’t answer those questions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses early resale and portfolio returns, but does not mention management fees or fees for arranging investments.

r002.rationale: It says excitement about the technology does not establish economic viability, but does not say AI hype makes large investments sound plausible.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention pension funds or managers expecting to leave before investments collapse.
